protections.label: An emergency room visit
protections.detail: If your plan covers emergency care, neither the hospital, nor the providers who treated you there, nor an air ambulance that brought you may charge you more than your in-network cost-sharing rate. This covers hospital emergency rooms, independent freestanding emergency departments, and any hospital department where you get post-stabilization services.

protections.label: Care to stabilize you after an emergency
protections.detail: Post-stabilization services are protected in most cases, whether you get them in the emergency room or in another department of the hospital. An out-of-network provider may ask you to sign a notice and consent form for this care; signing gives the protection up.

protections.label: Non-emergency care at an in-network facility
protections.detail: An out-of-network provider who treats you during a visit to an in-network hospital, hospital outpatient department, or ambulatory surgical center may not balance-bill you. This does not extend to other settings, such as a doctor's office that is not a hospital outpatient department, and it does not apply if the facility itself was out-of-network.

protections.label: Air ambulance services
protections.detail: An out-of-network air ambulance provider may not charge you more than your in-network cost-sharing rate.

exclusions.label: Ground ambulance
exclusions.detail: Ground ambulance services are generally not covered by the No Surprises Act's billing protections and may still charge out-of-network rates, unless a state law says otherwise.

exclusions.label: Vision-only and dental-only plans
exclusions.detail: The protections generally do not apply to vision-only or dental-only insurance, though they may apply where vision or dental benefits are part of your health plan.

exclusions.label: Short-term limited-duration plans and health care sharing ministries
exclusions.detail: Services covered by these plans are not subject to the No Surprises Act's billing protections.

exclusions.label: Fixed indemnity excepted-benefit plans, such as hospital indemnity insurance
exclusions.detail: Services covered by these plans are not part of the No Surprises Act's billing protections.

exclusions.label: Medicare, Medicaid, Indian Health Service, Veterans Affairs, and TRICARE
exclusions.detail: These programs already protect you from some unexpected out-of-network bills under their own rules, so the No Surprises Act's protections are not the ones that apply. The federal help desk can still help with a billing problem.

waiver.label: A notice and consent form gives the protection up
waiver.detail: For scheduled out-of-network care, or for post-stabilization care, a provider may ask you to sign a notice and consent form. Signing means you agree to be treated out-of-network and give up your protection from a surprise bill, and you will likely pay more. Signing is your choice; a provider may refuse the non-emergency care if you decline, in which case you can reschedule with an in-network provider.

uninsured.detail: If you are uninsured or are not using your insurance, a provider must generally give you a good faith estimate of what your care will cost when you schedule at least 3 business days in advance, or whenever you ask for one. You may be able to dispute the bill if it is at least $400 more than that estimate.

channels.label: No Surprises Help Desk — 1-800-985-3059
channels.note: Free, 7 days a week, with language support. Call with a question or to submit a complaint about a provider, facility, or insurer.

channels.label: CMS: find an action plan for your medical bill
channels.note: Answer a few questions and get the steps that fit your situation.

channels.label: CMS: dispute a medical bill
channels.note: The patient-provider dispute resolution process, for a bill at least $400 above a good faith estimate.

citation.sourceDocument: CMS, Medical bill rights — the No Surprises Act (effective 2022-01-01)
citation.sourceNote: Transcribed from the CMS consumer pages 'Medical bill rights' and 'Know your rights with insurance', which state the three protected situations (emergency room visits; non-emergency care related to a visit to an in-network hospital, hospital outpatient department, or ambulatory surgical center; air ambulance services), the exclusions (ground ambulance, vision-only and dental-only plans, short-term limited-duration and health care sharing ministry plans, fixed indemnity excepted-benefit plans), the notice-and-consent waiver, and the uninsured good-faith-estimate route (3 business days' advance scheduling; a bill at least $400 above the estimate may be disputed). No dollar figure here is a benchmark price: the Act sets who may bill you, not what care costs.
